desc:
You have bags of balls; bag i holds bags[i] balls. In one operation you take any bag and split it into two bags, each holding at least one ball (the two counts add up to the original). You may do at most maxOps operations.

The penalty is the number of balls in the largest bag. Return the smallest penalty you can reach.

Example: bags = [9], maxOps = 2. Split 9 into 6 + 3, then 6 into 3 + 3 to get bags 3, 3, 3 and penalty 3.
hints: Imagine the final penalty were at most x. How many splits does one bag of size b need so that all its pieces are at most x?
It needs ceil(b / x) - 1 splits: cut off pieces of size x until the rest fits. Summing over all bags gives the total number of operations required for penalty x, and it only decreases as x grows.
Binary search x in [1, max(bags)] for the smallest value whose required operations do not exceed maxOps.
editorial: Let need(x) = sum(ceil(b / x) - 1) be the minimum number of operations that make every bag hold at most x balls. A bag of size b ends up in at least ceil(b / x) pieces, hence at least that many minus one splits, and cutting x-sized pieces off achieves exactly this bound. Bags are independent, so the sum is exact.
need is non-increasing in x and need(max(bags)) = 0, so the answer is the smallest x with need(x) ≤ maxOps. Binary search gives O(n log max(bags)) time and O(1) space.
